claim: Reactivated inhibitory avoidance (IA) memory is enhanced through reconsolidation under conditions in which memory extinction is not induced.
source: Here, we show that reactivated inhibitory avoidance (IA) memory is enhanced through reconsolidation under conditions in which memory extinction is not induced.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing increased crossover latency at PR-LTM compared to Reactivation in vehicle-treated groups (Figure 1A-C), and by the experimental design that discriminates reconsolidation from extinction phases.

claim: Memory enhancement is mediated by neurons in the amygdala, hippocampus, and medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC).
source: This memory enhancement is mediated by neurons in the amygdala, hippocampus, and medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) through the simultaneous activation of calcineurin-induced proteasome-dependent protein degradation and cAMP responsive element binding protein-mediated gene expression.
evidence: Supported by c-fos and Arc expression data in these brain regions (Figure 2A-D), micro-infusion experiments showing effects of protein synthesis inhibition (Figure 2E-G), and proteasome inhibition experiments (Figure 3G-I).

claim: Memory enhancement involves calcineurin-induced proteasome-dependent protein degradation.
source: This memory enhancement is mediated by neurons in the amygdala, hippocampus, and medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) through the simultaneous activation of calcineurin-induced proteasome-dependent protein degradation and cAMP responsive element binding protein-mediated gene expression.
evidence: Supported by data showing increased Ub-Lys48 expression after reactivation (Figure 3A-F), effects of proteasome inhibitor β-lac (Figure 3G-I), and effects of calcineurin inhibitor FK506 (Figure 5A-I).

claim: Memory enhancement involves CREB-mediated gene expression.
source: This memory enhancement is mediated by neurons in the amygdala, hippocampus, and medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) through the simultaneous activation of calcineurin-induced proteasome-dependent protein degradation and cAMP responsive element binding protein-mediated gene expression.
evidence: Supported by CREBIR transgenic mouse experiments showing that inhibition of CREB-mediated transcription disrupts memory reconsolidation/enhancement (Figure 1G), and c-fos expression data (Figure 2A-D).

claim: The amygdala is required for memory reconsolidation and enhancement.
source: Interestingly, the amygdala is required for memory reconsolidation and enhancement, whereas the hippocampus and mPFC are required for only memory enhancement.
evidence: Supported by micro-infusion experiments showing that protein synthesis inhibition in the amygdala disrupts reactivated IA memory (Figure 2E), while inhibition in hippocampus or mPFC only blocks enhancement (Figure 2F,G).

claim: The hippocampus and mPFC are required for only memory enhancement, not reconsolidation.
source: Interestingly, the amygdala is required for memory reconsolidation and enhancement, whereas the hippocampus and mPFC are required for only memory enhancement.
evidence: Supported by data showing that protein synthesis inhibition in hippocampus or mPFC blocks enhancement but not reconsolidation (Figure 2F,G), and that mice display comparable enhancement at PR-LTM-2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).

claim: Memory enhancement triggered by retrieval utilizes distinct mechanisms from strengthening IA memory by additional learning.
source: Furthermore, memory enhancement triggered by retrieval utilizes distinct mechanisms to strengthen IA memory by additional learning that depends only on the amygdala.
evidence: Supported by data showing that protein synthesis inhibition in hippocampus or mPFC does not affect enhancement by additional training (Figure 4C,D), in contrast to enhancement by retrieval which requires these regions (Figure 2F,G).

claim: The VEH group displayed significantly increased crossover latency in Reactivation (398.9 ± 48.31 s) compared to Training (19.7 ± 1.68 s).
source: The control group (treated with vehicle, VEH) displayed significantly increased crossover latency in Reactivation (398.9 ± 48.31 s) compared to Training (19.7 ± 1.68 s), indicating that the mice formed and retrieved IA memory (Figure 1A).
evidence: Direct experimental measurement reported in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The VEH group displayed significantly increased crossover latency at PR-LTM (1553.5 ± 193.81 s) compared to Reactivation.
source: Interestingly, the VEH group displayed further and significantly increased crossover latency at PR-LTM (1553.5 ± 193.81 s) compared to Reactivation, suggesting that memory retrieval enhanced IA memory in our experimental condition.
evidence: Direct experimental measurement reported in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Memory retrieval enhanced IA memory in the experimental condition.
source: Interestingly, the VEH group displayed further and significantly increased crossover latency at PR-LTM (1553.5 ± 193.81 s) compared to Reactivation, suggesting that memory retrieval enhanced IA memory in our experimental condition.
evidence: Inferred from the significant increase in crossover latency at PR-LTM compared to Reactivation in vehicle-treated animals.

claim: The ability of retrieval to enhance memories is consistent with previous work (Gordon, 1981).
source: This ability of retrieval to enhance memories is consistent with previous work (Gordon, 1981).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gordon, 1981.

claim: Previous studies have shown that the inhibition of protein synthesis immediately after re-exposure to the light compartment disrupts reconsolidation of IA memory (Milekic and Alberini, 2002; Milekic et al., 2007).
source: Previous studies have shown that the inhibition of protein synthesis immediately after re-exposure to the light compartment disrupts reconsolidation of IA memory (Milekic and Alberini, 2002; Milekic et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Milekic and Alberini, 2002 and Milekic et al., 2007.

claim: The ANI group showed decreased crossover latency at PR-LTM compared to Reactivation.
source: The ANI group showed decreased crossover latency at PR-LTM compared to Reactivation, although the VEH and ANI groups showed comparable crossover latency at Reactivation, suggesting that the inhibition of protein synthesis disrupted IA memory.
evidence: Direct experimental measurement shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The inhibition of protein synthesis disrupted IA memory.
source: The ANI group showed decreased crossover latency at PR-LTM compared to Reactivation, although the VEH and ANI groups showed comparable crossover latency at Reactivation, suggesting that the inhibition of protein synthesis disrupted IA memory.
evidence: Inferred from the decreased crossover latency in ANI-treated animals at PR-LTM compared to Reactivation.

claim: Memory retrieval induces reconsolidation.
source: These results suggest that memory retrieval induces reconsolidation, raising the intriguing hypothesis that memory enhancement may be mediated by reconsolidation.
evidence: Inferred from the effects of protein synthesis inhibition on reactivated memory.

claim: Memory enhancement may be mediated by reconsolidation.
source: These results suggest that memory retrieval induces reconsolidation, raising the intriguing hypothesis that memory enhancement may be mediated by reconsolidation.
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis based on the experimental observations.

claim: The enhancement associated with the reconsolidation of fear memory was not transient or specific to the age of the memory.
source: These results indicate that the enhancement associated with the reconsolidation of fear memory was not transient or specific to the age of the memory.
evidence: Supported by experiments performed at 3 or 7 days after training showing similar enhancement patterns (Figure 1B,C).

claim: Re-exposure to the light compartment for 3 min resulted in the enhancement and disruption, respectively, of the reactivated memory in VEH and ANI groups.
source: In contrast, re-exposure of the VEH and ANI groups to the light compartment for 3 min resulted in the enhancement and disruption, respectively, of the reactivated memory compared to the controls (0 min (no) re-exposure groups in Reactivation and control group re-exposed 24 hr after training, respectively).
evidence: Direct experimental measurement shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Memory enhancement is associated with memory reconsolidation.
source: Taken together, our observations suggest that memory enhancement is associated with memory reconsolidation.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments showing enhancement after retrieval and its sensitivity to protein synthesis inhibition.

claim: A significant positive correlation of crossover latency was observed between Reactivation and PR-LTM (r2 = 0.646).
source: We observed a significant positive correlation of crossover latency between Reactivation and PR-LTM (Figure 1E).
evidence: Direct statistical analysis of data from 96 mice shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Longer reactivation of IA memory results in increased enhancement of this memory.
source: These observations indicate that longer reactivation of IA memory results in increased enhancement of this memory and strongly support our conclusion that IA memory is enhanced after retrieval.
evidence: Inferred from the positive correlation between crossover latency at Reactivation and PR-LTM.

claim: No correlation of crossover latency was observed between Training and Reactivation.
source: It is important to note that no correlation of crossover latency was observed between Training and Reactivation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), indicating that enhancement of IA memory is associated with memory retrieval of this memory.
evidence: Direct statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Enhancement of IA memory is associated with memory retrieval of this memory.
source: It is important to note that no correlation of crossover latency was observed between Training and Reactivation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), indicating that enhancement of IA memory is associated with memory retrieval of this memory.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of correlation between Training and Reactivation, contrasted with the correlation between Reactivation and PR-LTM.

claim: Memory reactivation in the dark compartment induces long-term memory extinction that requires new gene expression.
source: These observations indicate that memory reactivation in the dark compartment induces long-term memory extinction that requires new gene expression.
evidence: Supported by data showing decreased crossover latency in VEH group and blockade by ANI when mice stayed in dark compartment for 3 min (Figure 1F).

claim: The IA task enables discrimination between the reconsolidation and extinction phases at the time point when the mice enter the dark compartment from the light compartment.
source: Thus, consistent with our hypothesis, the IA task enables us to discriminate between the reconsolidation and extinction phases at the time point when the mice enter the dark compartment from the light compartment.
evidence: Supported by experimental design and data showing that extinction only occurs when mice enter and stay in the dark compartment (Figure 1F).

claim: Previous studies indicated that cAMP responsive element binding protein (CREB)-mediated transcription is required for the reconsolidation of reactivated fear memory (Kida et al., 2002; Mamiya et al., 2009).
source: Previous studies indicated that cAMP responsive element binding protein (CREB)-mediated transcription is required for the reconsolidation of reactivated fear memory (Kida et al., 2002; Mamiya et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kida et al., 2002 and Mamiya et al., 2009.

claim: CREB-mediated transcription is required for the reconsolidation/enhancement of IA memory.
source: These observations suggest that CREB-mediated transcription is required for the reconsolidation/enhancement of IA memory.
evidence: Supported by CREBIR transgenic mouse experiments showing disrupted memory in TAM-treated CREBIR mice (Figure 1G).

claim: Significant increases in the number of c-fos-positive cells were observed in the lateral (LA) and basolateral amygdala (BA), CA1 and CA3 regions of the hippocampus, and prelimbic (PL) and infralimbic (IL) regions of the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) in the T/R group compared to the other control groups.
source: Significant increases in the number of c-fos-positive cells were observed in the lateral (LA) and basolateral amygdala (BA), CA1 and CA3 regions of the hippocampus, and prelimbic (PL) and infralimbic (IL) regions of the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), but not in the central amygdala (CeA) regions or hippocampal dentate gyrus (DG) area, in the T/R group compared to the other control groups (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: Direct immunohistochemical measurements shown in Figure 2A-D.

claim: There was no increase in c-fos expression in the central amygdala (CeA) regions or hippocampal dentate gyrus (DG) area in the T/R group.
source: Significant increases in the number of c-fos-positive cells were observed in the lateral (LA) and basolateral amygdala (BA), CA1 and CA3 regions of the hippocampus, and prelimbic (PL) and infralimbic (IL) regions of the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), but not in the central amygdala (CeA) regions or hippocampal dentate gyrus (DG) area, in the T/R group compared to the other control groups (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: Direct immunohistochemical measurements shown in Figure 2A-D.

claim: There was no increase in c-fos expression in the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), visual cortex (VC), temporal cortex (TC), perirhinal cortex (PRh), or entorhinal cortex (EC) regions of the T/R group.
source: In contrast, there was no increase in c-fos expression in the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), visual cortex (VC), temporal cortex (TC), perirhinal cortex (PRh), or entorhinal cortex (EC) regions of the T/R group (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Direct immunohistochemical measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Significant increases in Arc expression were observed in the amygdala (LA and BA), hippocampus (CA1 and CA3), and mPFC (PL and IL) in the T/R group compared to the other control groups.
source: Similarly, significant increases in Arc expression were observed in the amygdala (LA and BA), hippocampus (CA1 and CA3), and mPFC (PL and IL) in the T/R group compared to the other control groups (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Direct immunohistochemical measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Significant positive correlations of the number of c-fos positive cells were observed between the amygdala (LA and BA), hippocampus (CA1 and CA3), and mPFC (PL and IL).
source: Interestingly, significant positive correlations of the number of c-fos positive cells were observed between the amygdala (LA and BA), hippocampus (CA1 and CA3), and mPFC (PL and IL) (Table 1), suggesting that c-fos expression in these regions was activated synchronously in response to memory reactivation.
evidence: Direct statistical analysis of correlations shown in Table 1.

claim: c-fos expression in the amygdala, hippocampus, and mPFC was activated synchronously in response to memory reactivation.
source: Interestingly, significant positive correlations of the number of c-fos positive cells were observed between the amygdala (LA and BA), hippocampus (CA1 and CA3), and mPFC (PL and IL) (Table 1), suggesting that c-fos expression in these regions was activated synchronously in response to memory reactivation.
evidence: Inferred from the positive correlations of c-fos expression between brain regions.

claim: Significant positive correlations were observed between crossover latency and the number of c-fos-positive cells.
source: Significant positive correlations were also observed between crossover latency and the number of c-fos-positive cells (Table 2).
evidence: Direct statistical analysis shown in Table 2.

claim: The increase in crossover latency at PR-LTM compared to Reactivation is associated with the synchronized induction of c-fos in the amygdala, hippocampus, and mPFC.
source: Taken together with the finding shown in Figure 1E, our observations suggest that the increase in crossover latency at PR-LTM compared to Reactivation is associated with the synchronized induction of c-fos in the amygdala, hippocampus, and mPFC.
evidence: Inferred from the correlations between c-fos expression, crossover latency at Reactivation, and enhancement at PR-LTM.

claim: Micro-infusion of ANI into the amygdala resulted in the disruption of the reactivated IA memory.
source: Similarly with the results for the systemic injection of ANI (Figure 1A), inhibition of protein synthesis in the amygdala resulted in the disruption of the reactivated IA memory (Figure 2E).
evidence: Direct experimental measurement shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Protein synthesis inhibition in the hippocampus or mPFC failed to disrupt the reactivated IA memory, but blocked its enhancement.
source: Interestingly, protein synthesis inhibition in the hippocampus or mPFC failed to disrupt the reactivated IA memory, but blocked its enhancement (Figure 2F,G); the ANI groups displayed comparable crossover latency between Reactivation and PR-LTM.
evidence: Direct experimental measurements shown in Figure 2F,G.

claim: Protein synthesis inhibition in both the hippocampus and mPFC blocked the enhancement of IA memory, but did not disrupt IA memory.
source: It is important to note that protein synthesis inhibition in both the hippocampus and mPFC blocked the enhancement of IA memory, but did not disrupt IA memory; furthermore, mice infused with ANI to the hippocampus or mPFC displayed a comparable enhancement of IA memory at PR-LTM-2 at 48 hr after PR-LTM-1 compared to the VEH group at PR-LTM-1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Direct experimental measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The inhibition of protein synthesis in the hippocampus or mPFC at Reactivation simply blocks the enhancement of IA memory without modulating it.
source: Thus, these observations suggest that the inhibition of protein synthesis in the hippocampus or mPFC at Reactivation simply blocks the enhancement of IA memory without modulating it.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that ANI-treated mice show comparable enhancement at a later time point (PR-LTM-2).

claim: Protein synthesis in the amygdala, but not the hippocampus, is required for the reconsolidation of IA memory (Taubenfeld et al., 2001; Milekic et al., 2007).
source: These results are consistent with a previous finding that protein synthesis in the amygdala, but not the hippocampus, is required for the reconsolidation of IA memory (Taubenfeld et al., 2001; Milekic et al., 2007), but more interestingly, suggest distinct roles for the amygdala and hippocampus/mPFC in the enhancement and reconsolidation of IA memory; new gene expression in the amygdala is required for the reconsolidation and enhancement of IA memory, while new gene expression in the hippocampus and mPFC is required only for its enhancement.
evidence: Supported by citations to Taubenfeld et al., 2001 and Milekic et al., 2007.

claim: New gene expression in the amygdala is required for the reconsolidation and enhancement of IA memory, while new gene expression in the hippocampus and mPFC is required only for its enhancement.
source: These results are consistent with a previous finding that protein synthesis in the amygdala, but not the hippocampus, is required for the reconsolidation of IA memory (Taubenfeld et al., 2001; Milekic et al., 2007), but more interestingly, suggest distinct roles for the amygdala and hippocampus/mPFC in the enhancement and reconsolidation of IA memory; new gene expression in the amygdala is required for the reconsolidation and enhancement of IA memory, while new gene expression in the hippocampus and mPFC is required only for its enhancement.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects of protein synthesis inhibition in these brain regions (Figure 2E-G).

claim: Serine 831 (Ser831) and serine 845 (Ser845) of GluA1 are phosphorylated by LTP induction or dephosphorylated after LTD induction, respectively.
source: The α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptor (AMPAR) GluA1 subunit undergoes distinct phosphorylation and dephosphorylation following the induction of long-term potentiation (LTP) and long-term depression (LTD) (Lee et al., 2000); serine 831 (Ser831) and serine 845 (Ser845) are phosphorylated by LTP induction or dephosphorylated after LTD induction, respectively.
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2000 and established knowledge about AMPAR phosphorylation.

claim: Phosphorylation of GluA1 alters the function of AMPAR and contributes to the expression of LTP and LTD.
source: This phosphorylation is thought to alter the function of AMPAR and contribute to the expression of LTP and LTD.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about AMPAR function and synaptic plasticity.

claim: Significant increases in Ser831 and Ser845 phosphorylation were observed in the amygdala, hippocampus, and mPFC regions of the T/R groups compared to the control groups at 30 min after Reactivation.
source: Significant increases in Ser831 and Ser845 phosphorylation were observed in the amygdala, hippocampus, and mPFC regions of the T/R groups compared to the control groups (Figure 2H,I).
evidence: Direct western blot measurements shown in Figure 2H,I.

claim: Increases in Ser831 and Ser845 phosphorylation in the T/R groups peaked at 30 min and returned to basal levels by 180 min after Reactivation.
source: Furthermore, time course analyses indicated that increases in Ser831 and Ser845 phosphorylation in the T/R groups peaked at 30 min and returned to basal levels by 180 min after Reactivation (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Direct western blot time course measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Synaptic plasticity was changed in the amygdala, hippocampus, and mPFC when IA memory was reconsolidated/enhanced.
source: Our observations that Ser831 and Ser845 phosphorylation was induced in the amygdala, hippocampus, and mPFC following Reactivation suggest that synaptic plasticity was changed in these regions when IA memory was reconsolidated/enhanced.
evidence: Inferred from the phosphorylation of GluA1 at sites associated with LTP.

claim: Proteasome-dependent protein degradation plays critical roles in the destabilization of reactivated contextual fear memory (Lee et al., 2008).
source: A previous study showed that proteasome-dependent protein degradation plays critical roles in the destabilization of reactivated contextual fear memory (Lee et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2008.

claim: Significant increases in the number of Ub-Lys48-positive cells were observed in the LA and BA of the amygdala, CA1 and CA3 of the hippocampus, and PL and IL of the mPFC in the T/R group.
source: Interestingly, significant increases in the number of Ub-Lys48-positive cells were observed in the same regions of the T/R group where c-fos was induced (Figure 3A–F).
evidence: Direct immunohistochemical measurements shown in Figure 3A-F.

claim: More than 70–80% of the c-fos-positive neurons of the T/R group were also Ub-Lys48-positive.
source: Most importantly, more than 70–80% of the c-fos-positive neurons of the T/R group were also Ub-Lys48-positive (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: Direct immunohistochemical co-localization measurements shown in Figure 3D-F.

claim: Gene expression and proteasome-dependent degradation were induced in the same neurons following IA memory retrieval.
source: These observations indicate that gene expression and proteasome-dependent degradation were induced in the same neurons following IA memory retrieval, suggesting that IA memory is reconsolidated/enhanced through gene expression and protein degradation in the same neurons.
evidence: Inferred from the co-localization of c-fos and Ub-Lys48 in the same neurons.

claim: IA memory is reconsolidated/enhanced through gene expression and protein degradation in the same neurons.
source: These observations indicate that gene expression and proteasome-dependent degradation were induced in the same neurons following IA memory retrieval, suggesting that IA memory is reconsolidated/enhanced through gene expression and protein degradation in the same neurons.
evidence: Inferred from the co-localization data and the functional effects of inhibiting these processes.

claim: Micro-infusions of β-lac into the amygdala, mPFC, or hippocampus blocked the enhancement of IA memory.
source: Interestingly, micro-infusions of β-lac into the amygdala, mPFC, or hippocampus blocked the enhancement of IA memory, indicating that activating proteasome-dependent protein degradation in these brain regions is required for the enhancement of IA memory.
evidence: Direct experimental measurements shown in Figure 3G-I.

claim: Activating proteasome-dependent protein degradation in the amygdala, mPFC, and hippocampus is required for the enhancement of IA memory.
source: Interestingly, micro-infusions of β-lac into the amygdala, mPFC, or hippocampus blocked the enhancement of IA memory, indicating that activating proteasome-dependent protein degradation in these brain regions is required for the enhancement of IA memory.
evidence: Inferred from the effects of proteasome inhibitor β-lac on memory enhancement.

claim: A micro-infusion of β-lac with ANI into the amygdala prevented the disruption of IA memory by protein synthesis inhibition.
source: Furthermore, a micro-infusion of β-lac with ANI into the amygdala prevented the disruption of IA memory by protein synthesis inhibition (Figure 3G), suggesting that protein degradation in the amygdala is required for the destabilization of reactivated IA memory.
evidence: Direct experimental measurement shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Protein degradation in the amygdala is required for the destabilization of reactivated IA memory.
source: Furthermore, a micro-infusion of β-lac with ANI into the amygdala prevented the disruption of IA memory by protein synthesis inhibition (Figure 3G), suggesting that protein degradation in the amygdala is required for the destabilization of reactivated IA memory.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that blocking protein degradation prevents memory disruption by protein synthesis inhibition.

claim: IA memory is reconsolidated/enhanced in the amygdala through protein degradation and synthesis, whereas protein synthesis and degradation in the hippocampus and mPFC are required for the enhancement of IA memory.
source: Taken together, our observations suggest that IA memory is reconsolidated/enhanced in the amygdala through protein degradation and synthesis, whereas protein synthesis and degradation in the hippocampus and mPFC are required for the enhancement of IA memory.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects of protein synthesis and degradation inhibition in different brain regions.

claim: Memory reconsolidation mediates the strengthening of memories following additional training (re-learning) via the activation of proteasome-dependent protein degradation and gene expression (Lee, 2008).
source: A previous study using contextual fear conditioning showed that memory reconsolidation mediates the strengthening of memories following additional training (re-learning) via the activation of proteasome-dependent protein degradation and gene expression (Lee, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee, 2008.

claim: Additional training enhanced IA memory more than retrieval without a footshock.
source: Crossover latency increased dramatically in the VEH group at PR-LTM (3940 ± 571.5 s) at 48 hr after Training-2 compared to following Reactivation (without a footshock in Figure 1A), suggesting that additional training enhanced IA memory more than retrieval without a footshock.
evidence: Direct experimental measurement comparing crossover latency after additional training (Figure 4) versus retrieval alone (Figure 1A).

claim: Inhibition of protein synthesis in the amygdala disrupted IA memory after additional training.
source: Similarly with a previous report, inhibition of protein synthesis in the amygdala disrupted IA memory, whereas inhibition of proteasome-dependent protein degradation with or without protein synthesis inhibition blocked the enhancement and disruption induced by ANI, respectively, of IA memory (Figure 4B).
evidence: Direct experimental measurement shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Inhibition of proteasome-dependent protein degradation blocked the enhancement of IA memory by additional training.
source: Similarly with a previous report, inhibition of protein synthesis in the amygdala disrupted IA memory, whereas inhibition of proteasome-dependent protein degradation with or without protein synthesis inhibition blocked the enhancement and disruption induced by ANI, respectively, of IA memory (Figure 4B).
evidence: Direct experimental measurement shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The inhibition of protein synthesis in the hippocampus or mPFC did not affect the enhancement of IA memory by additional training.
source: More interestingly, in contrast to the results shown in Figure 3, the inhibition of protein synthesis in the hippocampus or mPFC did not affect the enhancement of IA memory by additional training (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: Direct experimental measurements shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Gene expression in the hippocampus and mPFC is required only for IA memory enhancement following retrieval, not additional training.
source: Taken together, our observations that gene expression in the hippocampus and mPFC is required only for IA memory enhancement following retrieval indicate that these brain regions contribute to the enhancement of fear memory following retrieval, but not additional training, and more importantly, memory enhancement by retrieval utilizes a mechanism distinct from that used for additional learning.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects of protein synthesis inhibition in hippocampus/mPFC on enhancement by retrieval versus additional training.

claim: The hippocampus and mPFC contribute to the enhancement of fear memory following retrieval, but not additional training.
source: Taken together, our observations that gene expression in the hippocampus and mPFC is required only for IA memory enhancement following retrieval indicate that these brain regions contribute to the enhancement of fear memory following retrieval, but not additional training, and more importantly, memory enhancement by retrieval utilizes a mechanism distinct from that used for additional learning.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects of protein synthesis inhibition in these regions on different types of memory enhancement.

claim: Memory enhancement by retrieval utilizes a mechanism distinct from that used for additional learning.
source: Taken together, our observations that gene expression in the hippocampus and mPFC is required only for IA memory enhancement following retrieval indicate that these brain regions contribute to the enhancement of fear memory following retrieval, but not additional training, and more importantly, memory enhancement by retrieval utilizes a mechanism distinct from that used for additional learning.
evidence: Inferred from the differential requirements for hippocampus/mPFC in enhancement by retrieval versus additional training.

claim: Protein synthesis inhibition in the hippocampus immediately after Training blocked the consolidation of IA memory (Taubenfeld et al., 2001; Zhang et al., 2011).
source: Furthermore, it is important to note that: (1) protein synthesis inhibition in the hippocampus immediately after Training blocked the consolidation of IA memory (Taubenfeld et al., 2001; Zhang et al., 2011; Figure 3—figure supplement 1);
evidence: Supported by citations to Taubenfeld et al., 2001 and Zhang et al., 2011, and data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Consolidation of IA memory was not affected by the inhibition of proteasome-dependent protein degradation in the hippocampus.
source: (2) this consolidation was not affected by the inhibition of proteasome-dependent protein degradation in the hippocampus (Figure 3—figure supplement 1);
evidence: Direct experimental measurement shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: An increase in c-fos, but not Ub-Lys48, in the hippocampus was observed when IA memory was consolidated (Zhang et al., 2011).
source: and (3) an increase in c-fos (Zhang et al., 2011), but not Ub-Lys48, in the hippocampus was observed when IA memory was consolidated (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2011 and data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The reconsolidation/enhancement observed in this study utilize a mechanism distinct from that used for additional learning and consolidation.
source: Taken together, these observations indicate that the reconsolidation/enhancement observed in this study utilize a mechanism distinct from that used for additional learning and consolidation.
evidence: Inferred from the differential requirements for protein degradation and synthesis in reconsolidation/enhancement versus consolidation and additional learning.

claim: Calcineurin (CaN) activation in the hippocampus is required for the extinction of contextual fear memory (de la Fuente et al., 2011).
source: Interestingly, a recent study showed that calcineurin (CaN) activation in the hippocampus is required for the extinction of contextual fear memory (de la Fuente et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to de la Fuente et al., 2011.

claim: The micro-infusion of FK506 into the amygdala blocked the disruption of reactivated IA memory by protein synthesis inhibition and enhancement of IA memory.
source: The micro-infusion of FK506 into the amygdala blocked the disruption of reactivated IA memory by protein synthesis inhibition and enhancement of IA memory (Figure 5A), whereas the infusion of FK506 into the hippocampus or mPFC blocked the enhancement of IA memory (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: Direct experimental measurement shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The infusion of FK506 into the hippocampus or mPFC blocked the enhancement of IA memory.
source: The micro-infusion of FK506 into the amygdala blocked the disruption of reactivated IA memory by protein synthesis inhibition and enhancement of IA memory (Figure 5A), whereas the infusion of FK506 into the hippocampus or mPFC blocked the enhancement of IA memory (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: Direct experimental measurements shown in Figure 5B,C.

claim: CaN activation in the amygdala is required for the destabilization and enhancement of IA memory.
source: These observations suggest that, similar to protein degradation, CaN activation in the amygdala is required for the destabilization and enhancement of IA memory, while CaN activation in the hippocampus and mPFC is required for the enhancement of IA memory.
evidence: Inferred from the effects of CaN inhibitor FK506 on memory reconsolidation and enhancement.

claim: CaN activation in the hippocampus and mPFC is required for the enhancement of IA memory.
source: These observations suggest that, similar to protein degradation, CaN activation in the amygdala is required for the destabilization and enhancement of IA memory, while CaN activation in the hippocampus and mPFC is required for the enhancement of IA memory.
evidence: Inferred from the effects of CaN inhibitor FK506 on memory enhancement.

claim: The systemic injection of FK506 blocked the disruption of the reactivated IA memory by protein synthesis inhibition and the enhancement of IA memory.
source: It is important to note that, similar to the results of the micro-infusions, the systemic injection of FK506 blocked the disruption of the reactivated IA memory by protein synthesis inhibition and the enhancement of IA memory (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Direct experimental measurement shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The T/R groups treated with or without FK506 showed a comparable increase in the number of c-fos-positive cells compared to the U/R groups.
source: The T/R groups treated with or without FK506 showed a comparable increase in the number of c-fos-positive cells compared to the U/R groups (Figure 5D–I), suggesting that CaN activation is not required for c-fos induction.
evidence: Direct immunohistochemical measurements shown in Figure 5D-I.

claim: CaN activation is not required for c-fos induction.
source: The T/R groups treated with or without FK506 showed a comparable increase in the number of c-fos-positive cells compared to the U/R groups (Figure 5D–I), suggesting that CaN activation is not required for c-fos induction.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that FK506 treatment does not affect c-fos induction.

claim: The T/R groups treated with FK506 did not show an increase in the number of Ub-Lys48-positive cells.
source: In contrast, the T/R groups treated with FK506 did not show an increase in the number of Ub-Lys48-positive cells; only the T/R groups treated with VEH showed significantly more Ub-Lys48-positive cells than the other groups (Figure 5D–I).
evidence: Direct immunohistochemical measurements shown in Figure 5D-I.

claim: The inhibition of CaN blocked the increase of Ub-Lys48-positive cells, but not c-fos-positive cells, in the amygdala, hippocampus, and mPFC.
source: Thus, the inhibition of CaN blocked the increase of Ub-Lys48-positive cells, but not c-fos-positive cells, in the amygdala, hippocampus, and mPFC.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects of FK506 on Ub-Lys48 versus c-fos expression.

source: It is important to note that similar results were observed using another CaN inhibitor, cyclosporine A (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Direct experimental measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: CaN functions as an upstream regulator of proteasome-dependent protein degradation, but not c-fos induction, when reactivated memory is reconsolidated/enhanced.
source: These observations suggest that CaN functions as an upstream regulator of proteasome-dependent protein degradation, but not c-fos induction, when reactivated memory is reconsolidated/enhanced.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that CaN inhibition blocks protein degradation but not gene expression.

claim: Retrieval has been thought to have a role in enhancing memory that requires activation of gene expression and signal transduction pathways such as mTOR (Gordon, 1981; Nader et al., 2000; Nader and Hardt, 2009; Inda et al., 2011; Pedroso et al., 2013).
source: Retrieval has been thought to have a role in enhancing memory that requires activation of gene expression and signal transduction pathways such as mTOR (Gordon, 1981; Nader et al., 2000; Nader and Hardt, 2009; Inda et al., 2011; Pedroso et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gordon, 1981; Nader et al., 2000; Nader and Hardt, 2009; Inda et al., 2011; Pedroso et al., 2013.

claim: The IA paradigm discriminates the reconsolidation and extinction phases at the time point when the mice enter a dark compartment from a light compartment.
source: In this study, we developed IA paradigms in which the retrieval of fear memory triggers reconsolidation without inducing memory extinction; the reconsolidation and extinction phases are discriminated at the time point when the mice enter a dark compartment from a light compartment.
evidence: Supported by experimental design and data showing differential effects of staying in dark compartment (Figure 1F).

claim: Memory retrieval enhances IA memory through reconsolidation.
source: Using this paradigm, we found that memory retrieval enhances IA memory through reconsolidation.
evidence: Supported by multiple experiments showing enhancement after retrieval and its sensitivity to reconsolidation manipulations.

claim: The enhancement of IA memory by retrieval required CREB-mediated gene expression and calcineurin-induced proteasome-dependent protein degradation not only in the amygdala but also in the hippocampus and mPFC.
source: In contrast to the mechanisms for the reinforcement of contextual fear memory by additional learning, the enhancement of IA memory by retrieval required CREB-mediated gene expression and calcineurin-induced proteasome-dependent protein degradation not only in the amygdala but also in the hippocampus and mPFC.
evidence: Supported by experiments with CREBIR mice, protein synthesis inhibition, proteasome inhibition, and calcineurin inhibition in these brain regions.

claim: IA memory retrieval was suggested to induce synaptic plasticity in the amygdala, hippocampus, and mPFC through the phosphorylation of AMPAR.
source: Consistently, IA memory retrieval was suggested to induce synaptic plasticity in these brain regions through the phosphorylation of AMPAR.
evidence: Supported by data showing increased phosphorylation of GluA1 at Ser831 and Ser845 in these regions (Figure 2H,I).

claim: An IA memory is enhanced/reconsolidated through the reactivation of memory circuits consisting of multiple brain regions including the amygdala, hippocampus, and mPFC.
source: These findings suggest that an IA memory is enhanced/reconsolidated through the reactivation of memory circuits consisting of multiple brain regions including the amygdala, hippocampus, and mPFC and that the amygdala plays central and distinct roles from the hippocampus and mPFC in the enhancement/reconsolidation of IA memory.
evidence: Inferred from the synchronized activation of these regions and their differential functional roles.

claim: The amygdala plays central and distinct roles from the hippocampus and mPFC in the enhancement/reconsolidation of IA memory.
source: These findings suggest that an IA memory is enhanced/reconsolidated through the reactivation of memory circuits consisting of multiple brain regions including the amygdala, hippocampus, and mPFC and that the amygdala plays central and distinct roles from the hippocampus and mPFC in the enhancement/reconsolidation of IA memory.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects of manipulations in these regions on reconsolidation versus enhancement.

claim: Gene expression is required for the re-stabilization (reconsolidation) of reactivated memory (Nader et al., 2000; Taubenfeld et al., 2001; Debiec et al., 2002; Kida et al., 2002).
source: A previous study showed that gene expression is required for the re-stabilization (reconsolidation) of reactivated memory, whereas proteasome-dependent protein degradation is required for its destabilization (Nader et al., 2000; Taubenfeld et al., 2001; Debiec et al., 2002; Kida et al., 2002, Lee et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nader et al., 2000; Taubenfeld et al., 2001; Debiec et al., 2002; Kida et al., 2002.

claim: Proteasome-dependent protein degradation is required for the destabilization of reactivated memory (Lee et al., 2008).
source: A previous study showed that gene expression is required for the re-stabilization (reconsolidation) of reactivated memory, whereas proteasome-dependent protein degradation is required for its destabilization (Nader et al., 2000; Taubenfeld et al., 2001; Debiec et al., 2002; Kida et al., 2002, Lee et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2008.

claim: The amygdaloid neurons reactivated by the retrieval of an IA memory activated proteasome-dependent protein degradation and gene expression.
source: We found that the amygdaloid neurons reactivated by the retrieval of an IA memory activated proteasome-dependent protein degradation and gene expression, suggesting that these reactivated neurons regulate the destabilization and re-stabilization of IA memory.
evidence: Supported by co-localization data showing c-fos and Ub-Lys48 in the same neurons (Figure 3).

claim: Reactivated neurons regulate the destabilization and re-stabilization of IA memory.
source: We found that the amygdaloid neurons reactivated by the retrieval of an IA memory activated proteasome-dependent protein degradation and gene expression, suggesting that these reactivated neurons regulate the destabilization and re-stabilization of IA memory.
evidence: Inferred from the co-activation of protein degradation and gene expression in the same neurons and their functional roles.

claim: Destabilization and re-stabilization are regulated independently at the early stages of the signal transduction pathways activated after memory retrieval.
source: Importantly, our finding that inhibition of CaN blocked proteasome-dependent protein degradation, but not gene expression, suggests that destabilization and re-stabilization are regulated independently at the early stages of the signal transduction pathways activated after memory retrieval.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects of CaN inhibition on protein degradation versus gene expression.

claim: The activation of proteasome-dependent protein degradation is not only required for the destabilization of a reactivated memory but also plays additional roles in the modification or alteration of memory without the induction of destabilization.
source: Furthermore, our finding that the activation of gene expression and proteasome-dependent protein degradation in the hippocampus and mPFC is required for the enhancement, but not reconsolidation, of an IA memory also suggests that the activation of proteasome-dependent protein degradation is not only required for the destabilization of a reactivated memory but also plays additional roles in the modification or alteration of memory without the induction of destabilization.
evidence: Inferred from the requirement for protein degradation in hippocampus/mPFC for enhancement without affecting reconsolidation.

claim: CB1, proteasome-dependent protein degradation, and CaN are required for not only the destabilization of reactivated fear memory but also the extinction of fear memory (Suzuki et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2008; de la Fuente et al., 2011).
source: Previous and current studies have shown that CB1, proteasome-dependent protein degradation, and CaN are required for not only the destabilization of reactivated fear memory but also the extinction of fear memory (Suzuki et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2008; de la Fuente et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Suzuki et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2008; de la Fuente et al., 2011.

claim: Destabilization and extinction, both of which are triggered by memory retrieval, share similar signal transduction cascades.
source: These findings suggest that destabilization and extinction, both of which are triggered by memory retrieval, share similar signal transduction cascades.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that the same molecules are required for both processes.
